ALEX: So. One billion dollars. AMD takes a one-billion-dollar quarterly charge connected to its AI chip supply agreements with OpenAI and Meta. Reuters has this. I want to make sure I understand what a charge actually is here, because it's not the same as losing a billion dollars, right?
RUFUS: Right. A charge in this context means AMD is recognizing a cost against its earnings in this quarter — costs embedded in fulfilling those supply commitments. It's not cash disappearing into a void, but it absolutely hits the bottom line.
JAMIE: And it's tied specifically to the agreements with OpenAI and Meta. Not just general business costs. This is the price of being their chip supplier.
ALEX: So AMD signed these deals, committed to supplying chips at a certain scale, and now the accounting of that commitment lands as a billion-dollar hit in one quarter.
RUFUS: That's the shape of it. And the reason it matters beyond AMD is that it shows you exactly what frontier AI infrastructure actually costs at the hardware level. This isn't the cloud bill. This is upstream of the cloud bill.
JAMIE: It's the foundation of the foundation.
ALEX: Okay. So who absorbs this? Does it come back around to me somehow? Like, does this end up in what I pay for a ChatGPT subscription?
RUFUS: Eventually, costs travel. But the more immediate question is whether AMD's margins can absorb this, or whether supply agreements at this scale become structurally challenging for the chipmaker itself.
JAMIE: And the thing I keep thinking about is — this is one chipmaker, one quarter. What does the aggregate look like across the whole semiconductor sector? Because OpenAI and Meta are not exclusive to AMD.
ALEX: They're shopping around.
JAMIE: Everyone is shopping around. And every one of those deals carries a version of this cost.
RUFUS: The editorial analysis flags that we should watch for similar supply-chain charges from other semiconductor companies. I think that's the right thing to track. AMD disclosed. Others may follow.
ALEX: Rufus, take us on location.
RUFUS: Picture the floor of a mid-sized investment bank on Wall Street this morning — not the triumphant kind of morning, the kind where someone is quietly updating a spreadsheet and their expression is doing something complicated. Because AMD's disclosure lands today and the question institutional investors are asking is not "is a billion dollars a lot" — of course it is — the question is whether this is a one-quarter anomaly or the new rhythm of doing business as a chip supplier to frontier AI. The Reuters report confirms the charge is tied to supply commitments to OpenAI and Meta. What it doesn't tell us yet is how AMD accounts for future agreements, or whether OpenAI and Meta are on the hook for any of that exposure. For the semiconductor sector, this is a signal. If you are supplying chips to the biggest AI labs on earth, the capital commitment required to do that is now visibly enormous, and it shows up in earnings.
JAMIE: And yet — and I want to push on this — AMD presumably signed these deals knowing the costs. This isn't a surprise to them.
RUFUS: Almost certainly not. The surprise is the visibility. It's disclosed. It's a number. It's on the record.
ALEX: Back to the wider story. Jamie, you asked whether this hardware race is producing better software or just more expensive silicon. Where do you land?
JAMIE: Honestly, both. The models are getting better. But the cost trajectory is not sustainable in its current form without either prices going up for users or margins getting squeezed hard for the suppliers.
RUFUS: Reuters notes the charge may be subject to future accounting adjustments, so we're not at the final number yet.
ALEX: So the billion-dollar question — literally — is whether this is the going rate from now on or whether it's a peak.
RUFUS: And we don't have enough evidence to answer that yet.
JAMIE: Which is uncomfortable.
RUFUS: Deeply. But honestly, so is the number.
ALEX: One thing I want to flag for anyone tracking their own AI spend or investment exposure: this is the clearest single data point we've seen on the hardware cost embedded in frontier AI agreements. AMD disclosed it. Watch the next earnings calls across the sector.
JAMIE: And watch whether OpenAI or Meta say anything about it publicly, because they're the other side of these agreements.
RUFUS: They won't. But watch anyway.

scenes.original:
ALEX: Our second story — and this one is for anyone who uses an AI platform and assumes that changing their password keeps them safe. It does not. Not anymore.
JAMIE: Tell them why.
ALEX: There's new malware — infostealers, they're called — that specifically targets authentication tokens for ChatGPT, Claude, and Codex. And the alarming part is that these tokens survive a standard password reset.
JAMIE: So explain what a token is for someone who hasn't thought about this before.
ALEX: Right. So when you log into an AI platform, the system gives your device a small piece of data called a session token. Think of it as a temporary key that proves you already authenticated. Your device shows that token on future requests instead of asking for your password every time. It's what keeps you logged in.
JAMIE: And malware can steal that key.
ALEX: Yes. And once it's stolen, the attacker can use it to access your AI sessions — your conversations, your API access — without ever knowing your password.
JAMIE: Which is why changing the password doesn't fix it. The stolen token is still valid.
RUFUS: This is what enterprise security teams call a session hijacking attack. It's not new as a technique. What's new is that it's being targeted specifically at AI platforms — ChatGPT, Claude, Codex. That targeting is deliberate. These are tools with API access, organizational data, code, workflows.
ALEX: So it's not someone reading your chatbot conversations for fun. The concern is enterprise.
RUFUS: Mostly. Though personal users are exposed too. If you've got API keys tied to your account, or if you're using Claude for anything sensitive at work, the token is a meaningful access point.
JAMIE: There's something almost ironic about this. We've spent months talking about how AI tools are more secure than older software because of the authentication layers. And the attack isn't breaking the authentication — it's going around it.
RUFUS: The door is fine. Someone took your key while you weren't looking.
ALEX: So what does someone actually do about this?
JAMIE: The practical answer is endpoint security — that's just what we call the security software running on your actual device. The token lives on your machine, so if your machine is compromised, the token is exposed. Keeping endpoint security updated is the first line.
RUFUS: Beyond that, some platforms allow you to manually revoke all active sessions. That's worth knowing how to do. If you suspect something is wrong, you're not waiting for the platform to fix it — you can terminate all active tokens yourself.
ALEX: So it's not just "change your password and move on."
JAMIE: It's never just that anymore. And honestly, it hasn't been for a while.
ALEX: Here's the thing that struck me most. These aren't sophisticated state-level attacks necessarily. Infostealers are a category of malware that can be rented, essentially, in certain underground markets. The barrier to running one of these attacks is lower than the value of what you can steal.
RUFUS: Which is the worst possible combination.
JAMIE: And AI platforms have become valuable enough that they're worth targeting. That's new. A year ago, your ChatGPT session wasn't worth much to a criminal. Now, with agentic tools, API access, organizational data flowing through these platforms — it's a meaningful target.
ALEX: So the picture is: old technique, new target, and the standard defensive reflex — reset password — doesn't work.
JAMIE: Review your sessions. Know how to revoke them. Keep endpoint security current. And if you're managing this for a team, make sure your IT policy covers AI platform sessions specifically, not just corporate email.
RUFUS: Enterprise liability on this is real. If a token is stolen and someone accesses your organization's AI environment, the question of who is responsible for that breach is not simple.
ALEX: Okay. Here's a moment someone could actually send to a friend who uses these tools. Picture your friend logged into Claude for work, using it every day. They're not worried because they have a strong password. But they haven't thought about the fact that the token sitting on their laptop is the actual key — and malware can take it without touching the password at all. Send them this story. Tell them to find the "active sessions" or "devices" section in their AI platform settings. It's usually there. They should know where it is before they need it.
JAMIE: That's the real takeaway. Know where the off switch is before something goes wrong.
RUFUS: Preventative sessions management. Not the most exciting Tuesday activity, but.
JAMIE: Better than the alternative Tuesday.
JAMIE: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Rufus, another hundred AI headlines before breakfast? People have actual work to do. How do they decide what deserves their attention?
RUFUS: With The Ledger, Jamie. A longer reading list is hardly a strategy. Five focused briefings help connect the news to decisions.
JAMIE: So The Ledger gives you a place to start asking better questions about your work and your team?
RUFUS: Precisely. The Ledger. Find the link in our show notes. Now, back to the discussion.

scenes.original:
ALEX: Our third story — and this one is legitimately fascinating to me. NVIDIA published a post this week describing how semiconductor companies are using AI agents and something called digital twins to speed up the work of designing and building chips. The source is NVIDIA, so it's vendor-authored — we should say that clearly. But the specific example they cite is Applied Materials using NVIDIA's Omniverse libraries. And the concept is worth understanding.
JAMIE: What's a digital twin? For real, in one sentence.
ALEX: A digital twin is a detailed simulation of a physical system — in this case, an entire semiconductor fabrication facility. You model the fab in software, and engineers can run experiments inside the simulation instead of on the actual factory floor.
JAMIE: So you test a process change in the virtual factory before you try it in the real one.
ALEX: Exactly. And NVIDIA says that's meaningful because physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive.
RUFUS: They are. Semiconductor fabrication is extraordinarily precise. A single process change — adjusting temperature, timing, chemical ratios — takes significant time and money to test physically. The idea of running those tests in simulation first is genuinely appealing to the industry.
JAMIE: Okay. But here's my question. NVIDIA is writing this post. NVIDIA makes the Omniverse platform that Applied Materials is using. So I'm inclined to treat this as interesting evidence of a direction, not proof that it's working at scale.
ALEX: That's fair.
RUFUS: Completely fair. The post does not include independent measured performance data — no yield improvement percentage, no time-saved figures. It's describing a workflow and citing a partner.
ALEX: Though Applied Materials is a real and significant company. If they're building digital twins of fabs using Omniverse, that's a real deployment, not a hypothetical.
JAMIE: Sure. But is it working? Is it producing chips faster? Is it reducing defects? Those questions aren't answered by this post.
RUFUS: Which is exactly the right frame. This is a direction that makes engineering sense. The measurement of whether it's actually moving the needle — that comes later.
ALEX: There's a beautiful recursion to this though. We spent story one on how expensive it is to supply AI chips. And now in story three we have AI being used to try to make chip manufacturing faster and cheaper. It's AI trying to fix its own supply chain.
JAMIE: Heh. It's very on-brand for 2026.
RUFUS: The ecosystem eating itself constructively.
ALEX: If this actually works — and again, we're taking NVIDIA's word on early directions here — the downstream implication is that fab throughput improves. More chips, potentially faster. Which matters a lot given that the AMD story this morning tells us demand is enormous.
RUFUS: The connection is real. Chip supply is a genuine constraint on AI development. Anything that shortens engineering cycles in fabs could relieve some of that pressure. Even modestly.
JAMIE: I want to know what "speeds up" actually means in fab terms. Is that weeks? Months? Because if a simulation saves two hours on a process that takes six months, the efficiency gain is real but not transformative.
ALEX: That's the number we don't have from this post.
RUFUS: And may not get for a while. These are complex systems. Measuring the impact of a simulation tool across a whole manufacturing cycle takes time to establish.
JAMIE: So what should listeners actually watch for?
RUFUS: Whether other major fab operators — TSMC, Samsung, Intel Foundry — adopt similar approaches. If this spreads beyond Applied Materials, that's a signal the industry finds it valuable, not just NVIDIA's story about one partner.
ALEX: And whether anyone publishes independent results. A yield improvement figure from a third party would be much more convincing than a vendor blog.
JAMIE: Which is not a criticism of the concept. It's just where the evidence is right now.
RUFUS: The concept is sound. The proof is pending.
ALEX: One more thing worth noting: the AI agents piece of this. NVIDIA isn't just describing simulation software — they're describing AI agents that help engineers get faster answers across design, testing, and manufacturing. That's a broader deployment than just running a 3D model of a factory.
JAMIE: That part is interesting because it implies the AI is making decisions or at minimum surfacing recommendations inside the engineering workflow. Not just visualizing the factory.
RUFUS: Which is a meaningful distinction. A simulation you look at versus an agent that tells you something — those are very different levels of integration.
ALEX: And we don't have enough detail from this post to know exactly where Applied Materials falls on that spectrum.
JAMIE: Useful direction. Unproven at scale. Worth watching.
ALEX: That's pretty much where we are.
